summary: This document describes a way to negotiate encrypt-then-MAC in TLS and DTLS in place of the existing MAC-then-encrypt approach. The older ordering has been the subject of several security vulnerabilities over the years.

plainLanguage.summary: When TLS protects a record, it first computes a fingerprint of the data and then encrypts the data and the fingerprint together. The fingerprint is supposed to prove the data was not altered, but in that order an attacker can work on the encrypted form and learn things they should not. This RFC lets the two ends agree during the handshake to compute the fingerprint over the encrypted data instead, and to check it before decrypting. That way the fingerprint covers everything the attacker can see and change.

questions: why is mac then encrypt insecure
subtitle: A TLS and DTLS extension that lets both sides switch to the safer order of encrypting first and adding the MAC afterwards.

tldr.problem: TLS and DTLS protect a record by computing a MAC over the plaintext, then encrypting the plaintext and the MAC together. That order, called MAC-then-encrypt, was regarded as safe when SSL was designed in the mid-1990s, but it has since been the subject of many vulnerabilities and attacks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a TLS extension, encrypt_then_mac, of type 22, that a client offers in its client hello and a server accepts in its server hello. Once both sides have exchanged it, the MAC is computed over the encrypted packet instead of the plaintext, and appended outside the encrypted data, and the receiver checks the MAC before decrypting anything.
tldr.outcome: The weaker construction is replaced without changing any cipher suite, because the switch is made with a single extension rather than with new cipher suites. A session that has negotiated it must not be renegotiated back down to the old order.

facts.label: Packet layout change
facts.value: The MAC is moved outside the encrypted data

today: RFC 7366 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. IANA has added the extension code point 22 to the TLS ExtensionType Values registry for it.

sections.title: The Problem with MAC-then-Encrypt
sections.content:
TLS and DTLS use a MAC-then-encrypt construction that was regarded as secure at the time the original Secure Socket Layer protocol was specified in the mid-1990s, but that is no longer regarded as secure. This construction, as used in TLS and later DTLS, has been the subject of numerous security vulnerabilities and attacks stretching over a period of many years. The RFC specifies a means of switching to the more secure encrypt-then-MAC construction as part of the TLS/DTLS handshake, replacing the current MAC-then-encrypt construction. In the document, MAC refers to Message Authentication Code.

The difference between the two constructions is the order of two operations on the record. In MAC-then-encrypt, the MAC is computed over the plaintext and is then encrypted along with the data. In encrypt-then-MAC, the data is encrypted first and the MAC is computed over the encrypted result. Because the attacker only ever sees the encrypted form, a MAC computed over the encrypted form cannot be manipulated in the way that a MAC over the plaintext can, and the receiver can check it before doing anything else with the record.
sections.plainLanguage:
TLS protects each piece of data in two steps. It computes a short fingerprint, called a MAC, over the data, and then encrypts the data and the fingerprint together into what goes on the wire. The receiver decrypts the lot and then checks the fingerprint.

The problem is that the fingerprint was made over the data before encryption, while the attacker only ever sees the encrypted form. That gap has been the source of a long series of attacks. This RFC swaps the two steps: the fingerprint is computed over the encrypted form and sent outside it, so the receiver can check the fingerprint first and stop before doing anything with the contents.

sections.title: Negotiating the Switch
sections.content:
The use of encrypt-then-MAC is negotiated with TLS and DTLS extensions. On connecting, the client includes the encrypt_then_mac extension in its client_hello if it wishes to use encrypt-then-MAC rather than the default MAC-then-encrypt. If the server is able to meet the requirement, it responds with encrypt_then_mac in its server_hello. The extension type value for this extension SHALL be 22, which is 0x16, and the extension_data field of the extension SHALL be empty. The client and server MUST NOT use encrypt-then-MAC unless both sides have successfully exchanged the encrypt_then_mac extensions.

Because the switch is made with an extension rather than with a new cipher suite, it applies to every cipher suite the two ends already agree on. If the client asks for it and the server does not send it back, the session simply continues with the default MAC-then-encrypt construction.
sections.plainLanguage:
The two ends agree on this during the handshake, using the same extension mechanism TLS already has for optional features. The client says in its opening message that it would like the safer order, and the server says in its reply that it agrees. The extension carries no data at all, only its presence.

Neither side may use the new order unless both have sent it, so an implementation that does not know the extension simply continues with the old behaviour and the connection still works.

sections.title: Why an Extension and Not New Cipher Suites
sections.content:
Using TLS and DTLS extensions to negotiate an overall switch is preferable to defining new cipher suites, because the latter would result in a Cartesian explosion of suites, potentially requiring every single existing suite to be duplicated with a new one that uses encrypt-then-MAC. The approach presented here requires just a single new extension type with a corresponding minimal-length extension sent by the client and the server.

Another possibility for introducing encrypt-then-MAC would be to make it part of TLS 1.3, but that would require the implementation and deployment of all of TLS 1.2 just to support a trivial code change in the order of encryption and MAC'ing. Deploying encrypt-then-MAC through the extension mechanism instead required changing less than a dozen lines of code in one implementation, not counting the handling for the new extension type, which was a further fifty or so lines.

The use of extensions precludes use with SSL 3.0, but anything still using that protocol, which is nearly two decades old, will be vulnerable to any number of other attacks anyway, so there seems little point in bending over backwards to accommodate SSL 3.0.
sections.plainLanguage:
The obvious alternative would have been to define a second version of every cipher suite, one that uses the new order. That would mean doubling the list of cipher suites for a change that has nothing to do with which algorithm is used.

Making the switch part of TLS 1.3 was also considered and rejected, because it would have meant deploying a whole new version of the protocol to change two lines of code. As an extension, the change was a dozen lines in one implementation, plus about fifty more to handle the new extension.

The cost is that SSL 3.0, which has no extension mechanism, cannot use it. The RFC notes that a protocol that old is vulnerable to many other attacks anyway.

sections.title: Applying Encrypt-then-MAC
sections.content:
Once the use of encrypt-then-MAC has been negotiated, the processing of TLS and DTLS records switches from the standard encrypt( data || MAC || pad ) to the new encrypt( data || pad ) || MAC, with the MAC covering the entire packet up to the start of the MAC value.

In TLS notation, the MAC calculation for TLS 1.0 without the explicit initialisation vector is MAC(MAC_write_key, seq_num + TLSCipherText.type + TLSCipherText.version + TLSCipherText.length + ENC(content + padding + padding_length)), and for TLS 1.1 and greater with an explicit IV it is MAC(MAC_write_key, seq_num + TLSCipherText.type + TLSCipherText.version + TLSCipherText.length + IV + ENC(content + padding + padding_length)). For DTLS the sequence number is replaced by the combined epoch and sequence number. The final MAC value is then appended to the encrypted data and padding. This calculation is identical to the existing one, with the single exception that the MAC is computed over the payload ciphertext rather than over the plaintext.

The overall TLS packet becomes a content type, a protocol version, a length, a generic block cipher fragment and an opaque MAC, and the equivalent DTLS packet adds an epoch and a 48-bit sequence number before the length. This is identical to the existing TLS and DTLS layout, with the only difference being that the MAC value is moved outside the encrypted data.

The note on the generic block cipher annotation means that this only applies to standard block ciphers that have distinct encrypt and MAC operations. It does not apply to generic stream ciphers, or to generic AEAD ciphers that already include integrity protection with the cipher. If a server receives an encrypt-then-MAC request extension from a client and then selects a stream or AEAD cipher suite, it MUST NOT send an encrypt-then-MAC response extension back to the client.

Decryption reverses the processing. The MAC SHALL be evaluated before any further processing such as decryption is performed, and if the MAC verification fails then processing SHALL terminate immediately. For TLS a fatal bad_record_mac MUST be generated, and for DTLS the record MUST be discarded and a fatal bad_record_mac MAY be generated. This immediate response to a bad MAC eliminates any timing channels that may be available through the use of manipulated packet data.

Some implementations may prefer to use a truncated MAC rather than a full-length one, in which case they MAY negotiate the use of a truncated MAC with the TLS truncated_hmac extension.
sections.plainLanguage:
After the switch, the record is built like this. The data is encrypted, with the padding as the original method requires, and the MAC is then computed over the whole encrypted packet, including the header fields and the sequence number, and appended after it. The MAC is computed in the same way as before, except that it now covers the encrypted bytes instead of the plain ones.

The packet layout barely changes. The MAC simply moves from inside the encrypted part to outside it.

On the receiving side the order of operations is what matters. The MAC is checked first, before any decryption, and if it does not match, the record is dropped at once. That removes the timing channels: an attacker cannot tell how far the processing got, because it stops immediately.

sections.title: What Happens at a Rehandshake
sections.content:
The status of encrypt-then-MAC against MAC-then-encrypt can potentially change during one or more rehandshakes. Implementations SHOULD retain the current session state across all rehandshakes for that session, so that if the mechanism for the current session is one thing, the renegotiated session uses the same thing. Although implementations SHOULD NOT change the state during a rehandshake, if they wish to be more flexible then the rules in the table apply.

When the current session uses MAC-then-encrypt and the renegotiated session also uses MAC-then-encrypt, there is no change. When the current session uses MAC-then-encrypt and the renegotiated session uses encrypt-then-MAC, the session is upgraded to encrypt-then-MAC. When the current session uses encrypt-then-MAC and the renegotiated session uses MAC-then-encrypt, that is an error. When the current session uses encrypt-then-MAC and the renegotiated session also uses encrypt-then-MAC, there is no change.

Implementations MUST NOT renegotiate a downgrade from encrypt-then-MAC to MAC-then-encrypt. A client or server that does not wish to implement the ability to change mechanism during a rehandshake can, as a client, not request a mechanism change, and as a server, deny the mechanism change.

These rules apply across potentially many rehandshakes. For example, if a session were in the encrypt-then-MAC state and a rehandshake selected an AEAD cipher suite, and a subsequent rehandshake then selected a MAC-then-encrypt cipher suite, that would be an error, because the renegotiation has resulted in a downgrade from encrypt-then-MAC to MAC-then-encrypt via the AEAD cipher suite.

If an upgrade from MAC-then-encrypt to encrypt-then-MAC is negotiated, the change takes place in the first message that follows the Change Cipher Spec message. All messages up to and including the Change Cipher Spec use MAC-then-encrypt, and the message that follows continues with encrypt-then-MAC.
sections.plainLanguage:
A connection can be re-keyed part way through, and the question is whether the new order can be changed at that point. The rule is that it can go up but not down. A session using the old order may move to the new one, but a session using the new one must not be allowed to fall back.

The rule holds across any number of re-keyings, so a detour through a cipher suite that has its own built-in integrity protection does not provide a way round it.

When the upgrade happens, it takes effect at a defined point: the messages up to and including the Change Cipher Spec still use the old order, and the first message after it uses the new one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defines encrypt-then-MAC as an improved security mechanism to replace the current MAC-then-encrypt one. Encrypt-then-MAC is regarded as more secure than the current mechanism and should mitigate or eliminate a number of attacks on it, provided that the instructions on MAC processing given in Section 3 are applied.

An active attacker who can emulate a client or server with extension intolerance may cause some implementations to fall back to older protocol versions that do not support extensions, which will in turn force a fallback to non-encrypt-then-MAC behaviour. A straightforward solution to this problem is to avoid fallback to older, less secure protocol versions. If fallback behaviour is unavoidable, then mechanisms to address this issue, which affects all capabilities negotiated by TLS extensions, are being developed by the TLS working group. Anyone concerned about this type of attack should consult the TLS working group documents for guidance on appropriate defence mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage:
The document's own judgement is that the new order is more secure and should remove a number of attacks on the old one, but only if the receiver checks the MAC before it decrypts anything.

One attack remains. An attacker can pretend to be an old implementation that does not understand extensions, which may push the real implementation back to an older version of the protocol that cannot use the new order. The fix is to stop falling back to older versions, and the RFC notes that the TLS working group is working on the general problem of extension downgrade, which affects every optional feature negotiated this way.

cells: The MAC is computed over the plaintext, then the data and the MAC are encrypted together
The data is encrypted first, then the MAC is computed over the encrypted result
The whole packet up to the start of the MAC value
Outside the encrypted data, appended after it
Before any decryption, and processing stops immediately if it fails

viz.caption: THE TWO CONSTRUCTIONS, AS THE RFC WRITES THEM

data.title: Record construction
data.code:
MAC-then-encrypt:  encrypt( data || MAC || pad )

Encrypt-then-MAC:  encrypt( data || pad ) || MAC

items.title: Extension type
items.text: 22, which is 0x16, in the TLS ExtensionType Values registry.

items.title: Who sends it
items.text: The client offers it in its client_hello, and the server accepts it in its server_hello.

items.title: When it applies
items.text: Only when both sides have exchanged the extension; otherwise the default order is used.
